title: Modern C++ Memory Management: Smart Pointers & Move Semantics
summary: Quick revision notes on replacing raw new/delete with RAII and smart pointers (unique_ptr, shared_ptr, weak_ptr), then move semantics, rvalue references, std::move and copy elision. Ends with a one-page cheat sheet.

chapters.title: RAII and the new/delete Problem
points: RAII: acquire a resource in a constructor, release it in the destructor; the destructor runs on every scope exit, including exceptions and early returns
Raw new/delete leaks on early return or exception: `auto p = new T; f(); delete p;` skips delete if f() throws
Mismatched forms are UB: `new[]` must pair with `delete[]`, `new` with `delete`, and `malloc` with `free`
Double delete and use-after-free are UB; set a freed pointer to nullptr is only a band-aid, not ownership
Rule of thumb: no naked new/delete in application code; a raw pointer or reference means non-owning observer, ownership lives in a RAII type

chapters.title: unique_ptr: Exclusive Ownership
points: `std::unique_ptr<T>` owns one object exclusively; zero overhead vs raw pointer with the default deleter, and it deletes automatically on destruction
Not copyable, only movable: `auto b = std::move(a);` leaves `a` null
Array form `unique_ptr<T[]>` uses delete[] and supports operator[]
Access API: `get()` borrows the raw pointer, `release()` gives up ownership without deleting, `reset(p)` deletes the old object and takes p
Pass by value to transfer ownership, by `T*` or `T&` to merely use it; return by value from factories and it moves automatically

chapters.title: shared_ptr, weak_ptr and make_shared
points: `shared_ptr` shares ownership via a control block holding strong count, weak count and deleter; the object is destroyed when strong count hits 0
Copy increments the count atomically; copying a shared_ptr is thread-safe for the control block but access to the pointee is not
Cycles (A holds shared_ptr to B and B to A) never reach 0 and leak; break them with `weak_ptr` for back-references
`weak_ptr` does not keep the object alive; use `if (auto sp = wp.lock())` to get a shared_ptr or null if expired, and `expired()` to check
Never build two shared_ptrs from the same raw pointer (two control blocks, double delete); use `enable_shared_from_this` and `shared_from_this()` inside a class

chapters.title: make_unique and make_shared
points: Prefer `std::make_unique<T>(args)` and `std::make_shared<T>(args)` over `new`; they avoid naming the type twice and are exception safe in argument lists
`make_shared` does one allocation for object and control block, so it is faster and more cache friendly than `shared_ptr<T>(new T)` which does two
Trade-off: with make_shared, memory of the object stays allocated until the last weak_ptr dies because it shares the block
make_* cannot use a custom deleter or brace-init lists directly, so fall back to the shared_ptr/unique_ptr constructor in those cases
Choose unique_ptr by default and convert to shared_ptr only when ownership is truly shared: `shared_ptr<T> s = std::move(u);`

chapters.title: Move Semantics, Rvalue References and Copy Elision
points: An lvalue has a name and an address; an rvalue is a temporary; `T&&` is an rvalue reference that binds to temporaries and enables stealing resources
`std::move(x)` is only a cast to `T&&`; it moves nothing itself, the move constructor or assignment does the transfer
A moved-from object is valid but unspecified: only destroy it or assign to it, do not read its value
Move constructor/assignment should steal pointers, null out the source and be `noexcept`, otherwise `std::vector` falls back to copying on reallocation
Do not write `return std::move(local);` because it blocks copy elision (RVO); returning the local by name lets the compiler elide or move; C++17 guarantees elision for prvalues like `return T{};`
A named `T&&` parameter is an lvalue inside the function; forward it with `std::forward<T>` in templates or `std::move` otherwise
Rule of zero: hold members as smart pointers or containers and write none of the five special members; if you define one, consider all (rule of five)

chapters.title: Smart Pointers and Move Cheat Sheet
points: Default choice table: unique_ptr for sole owner, shared_ptr for shared owner, weak_ptr for non-owning observer of shared, raw T*/T& for non-owning use
Creation: `make_unique<T>(...)`, `make_shared<T>(...)`; transfer: `std::move(up)`; check: `if (sp)`, `wp.lock()`
unique_ptr API: get, release, reset, swap; shared_ptr API: use_count, reset, get, lock via weak_ptr
Move rules: std::move is a cast, moved-from is valid-but-unspecified, mark moves noexcept, never `return std::move(local)`
Top pitfalls checklist: naked new, new[]/delete mismatch, shared_ptr cycles, two shared_ptrs from one raw pointer, reading a moved-from object
